meta.headline: Three things left, and one I got wrong.
meta.lede: Last round settled it: a **habit you keep**, title only to start, handed back as a one-page plan that also says what not to build. My offline question did not make sense — it is back below in plainer words, along with the abandoned-books problem you raised.
steps: Answer, change or reject each one
meta.closingAsk: Update the scope from these answers, then tell me what is still open.

scope.label: What we're trying to achieve
scope.text: A log you keep up: title only, logged in a tap or two, and it works in a tunnel.

scope.label: What we hand over
scope.text: A one-page build plan, readable on the train, that says what to build and what not to build.

scope.label: What's in and what's out
scope.text: Finished and abandoned books both go in. Entries can gain fields later. Still nothing social.

scope.label: How we know it's done
scope.text: Three taps or fewer to log a book, checked on day one, then still in use a month later.

scope.label: Fixed facts we work inside
scope.text: Phone, on the train, under six taps to log a book. No account, no feed, nobody else ever sees it.

context.title: What changed since last time
context.note: You cut the fields down to title only and asked whether you could add more later without losing anything. You can — but only if the answer to the first question below is the one I recommend.

items.desc: a habit, title only, a one-page plan with an explicit not-building list
the train problem, abandoned books, and what counts as working

questions.context: I asked this badly last time. Here it is in plainer terms: you are in a tunnel, you finish a book, you tap save. What should happen?
breakdown: It saves on the phone straight away, and you never see a difference.
It waits for signal, so you see an error and have to remember to come back.
questions.example: Notes on your phone works the first way — you type on a plane and it appears on your laptop later, without you doing anything.
questions.question: In a tunnel, what happens when you tap save?
questions.why: Saving on the phone first is how every app that survives a commute works, and the difference in build effort is about an afternoon.
questions.switchIf: Choose the second if your line has signal end to end and you would rather have this working sooner.

options.label: It saves, and you carry on
options.detail: Written to the phone; syncs later if it needs to.

options.label: It tells you to try later
options.detail: Simpler to build, and it fails where you read.

questions.context: You said abandoning happens more than finishing. That makes it a real part of the log, not an edge case, and it changes what the log means.
breakdown: Only finished books: the list stays a list of achievements.
Finished and abandoned: more honest, and the list becomes a record of your reading rather than your wins.
questions.question: Should abandoned books go in the log?
questions.why: You raised it unprompted, which usually means it matters, and a log that quietly omits most of your reading will feel wrong within a month.
questions.switchIf: Keep finished-only if what you want from this in a year is a list you feel good about.

options.label: Finished books only
options.detail: One kind of entry; nothing to decide.

options.label: Finished and abandoned
options.detail: One extra tap, and a truer record.

options.label: Track progress too
options.detail: Page counts and updates; back to six taps.

questions.context: You asked whether you can start with the title alone and add more later without losing what is already there. That depends on one decision, made now.
breakdown: Room left for more: entries can gain fields later and old ones stay readable.
Title only, fixed: simplest now, and adding a field later means rewriting the lot.
questions.example: If each entry is saved as a little labelled record rather than one line of text, adding a rating next year leaves every old entry exactly as it was.
questions.question: Should entries be able to gain fields later?
questions.why: It costs nothing today and it is the difference between adding a field in an evening and migrating a year of entries by hand.
questions.switchIf: Take the fixed version if you are fairly sure the title is all you will ever want.

options.label: Leave room to grow
options.detail: Add fields later; old entries still work.

options.label: Fix it at the title
options.detail: Simplest now, painful to change later.

questions.context: You cut the fields to title only, so the test I assumed no longer measures anything. What would tell you this worked?
breakdown: A tap count: measurable today, and it is the bar Goodreads failed.
Still using it in a month: the thing you actually care about, but you cannot check it now.
questions.question: What would tell you this worked?
questions.why: The tap count is the only one you can check the day it is built, and it is the exact thing that made you quit twice before.
questions.switchIf: Choose the month if you would rather judge this on the habit than on the mechanics.

options.label: Three taps or fewer
options.detail: Checkable the day it is finished.

options.label: Still using it in a month
options.detail: The real test, but you wait for it.

options.label: Both, in that order
options.detail: Taps now, the habit as the honest one.

questions.context: There is one failure worth naming now: the log is on your phone, and phones get lost. What happens then decides how much trust this thing deserves.
breakdown: A copy somewhere else: the log survives the phone, at the cost of some setup.
Phone only: nothing to set up, and losing the phone loses everything.
questions.question: What happens if you lose the phone?
questions.why: A year of reading is worth more than the ten minutes of setup, and knowing it is safe is part of what makes a habit stick.
questions.switchIf: Stay phone-only if you would rather not think about it until the log is worth protecting.

options.label: A copy somewhere else
options.detail: Survives the phone; a little setup once.

options.label: Phone only for now
options.detail: Nothing to set up; nothing to fall back on.
